one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reflects on Pope Francis's six-stop PH visit -- (1) officialdom led by PNoy in Malacañang (where, as a retired chief justice, CJ was invited), (2) priests at Manila Cathedral, (3) families at Mall of Asia, (4) typhoon survivors in Leyte, (5) youth at UST today, and (6) ordinary folks at Luneta -- before the Pope leaves for Rome tomorrow. The Pope is not meeting with tycoons, industrialists, and bankers. Is he anti-rich? Yes, but only against the greedy and the self-centered -- not against the rich who regard themselves as mere stewards of their wealth for the benefit of all, especially 'the naked, the imprisoned, the hungry and the homeless.' In Francis's own words, 'The Gospel does not condemn the wealthy, but the idolatry of wealth, the idolatry that makes people indifferent to the call of the poor.' And CJ adds: our Lord Jesus had rich disciples too, like Joseph of Arimathea who retrieved and buried His body after His crucifixion. In CJ's humble view, to be pro-poor it is not necessary to be anti-rich; in fact, an effective pro-poor program should include and inspire the rich to share their resources -- not by easy doles of crumbs that merely perpetuate the poor's dependence, but by empowering the poor to conquer poverty through education and entrepreneurship. This is precisely what the Jollibee Group Foundation has been doing through two flagship projects: Busog, Lusog, Talino (BLT) and the Farmers Entrepreneurship Program (FEP). During JGF's 10th-anniversary celebration days ago, its president Grace Tan Caktiong noted that although the state provides free elementary and high school education, she was 'horrified to learn' that despite this, the dropout rate was alarming -- and the 'most common and shocking reason' was HUNGER. To reduce dropout drastically, JGF started in 2007 its BLT program of feeding the poorest-of-the-poor pupils every school day. As of end-2014, BLT has reached over 1,000 schools nationwide and fed almost 200,000 pupils -- now the largest private-sector-led systematic school-feeding program in the country, with community participation mobilized by getting parents, teachers, and village elders to prepare and serve the free nutritious meals. To supply its 2,000+ fast-food outlets (Jollibee, Chow King, Mang Inasal, Greenwich, Red Ribbon, Burger King) with high-quality vegetables, potatoes, and calamansi, JFC noticed that small farmers had difficulty producing them. So in 2008, JGF launched FEP -- opening free training centers, providing access to finance, and linking farmers to institutional markets. Today 15 big institutions including JFC source their vegetable requirements directly from FEP-assisted small farmers, guaranteeing year-round profitability; over 900 farmers from 15 provinces have benefited by end-2014. Ms. Tan Caktiong explained that early on, she and her husband Tony (chair of both JFC and JGF) had given millions to charity without knowing exactly how the money was spent -- so they set up JGF to ensure funds are disbursed wisely and accounted for accurately. She resigned from involvement in the business conglomerate to concentrate as JGF president; planning originally to stay only three years, she has been so overwhelmed by the passion to help the poor that she devotes full time, without pay, to alleviating poverty. Even her husband Tony has given up his CEO position to devote more time to philanthropy and overall policymaking. They remind CJ of Bill and Melinda Gates, the world's richest couple, who quit their executive jobs in Microsoft Corp. to focus full-time on multibillion-dollar charity work for the world's poor. The Tan Caktiongs -- who control the giant JFC, ranked 10th-largest in market capitalization among the world's fast-food chains -- may not be as wealthy as the Gateses, but they are driven by the same passion and patience to help the poor. They are exemplars of Pope Francis' call for sharing time, talent and treasure with the least, last and lost. Incidentally, both JGF projects were recognized during the Asian Corporate Social Responsibility Awards Night -- BLT won for education and FEP for poverty alleviation, besting 109 entries from 15 Asian countries; JGF is the first organization to win two awards in the same year. A third project, FoodAID, was established by JGF immediately after Supertyphoon Yolanda hit the country in 2013, setting up mobile kitchens in severely affected communities and providing meals for one month to more than 162,000 survivors as well as to volunteers of various relief organizations.
